unit.title: Develop an understanding of concepts and application of optoelectronics technology

summary: This unit introduces optoelectronics: the devices that give out, detect or control light. You will learn what light is and how it is measured, how LEDs, light sensors, solar cells, optocouplers, displays and lasers work, and how to work out and build simple LED and light-sensing circuits on an extra-low-voltage bench supply. You will also learn to test the parts, find faults, work safely with bright light and lasers, and recognise where these devices are used in Jamaica.

blocks.p: **Optoelectronics** is the part of electronics that deals with devices that give out light (LEDs, lasers, displays), detect light (LDRs, photodiodes, phototransistors, solar cells) or use light to pass a signal (optocouplers and fibre optics). Electricians meet these devices every day: in LED lighting and signs, photocells on street and security lights, beams on automatic gates, solar panels and the control panels of machines. This unit is for Level 2 trainees and is done on extra-low-voltage circuits.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Describe visible, infrared and ultraviolet light, give wavelengths in nanometres, and use lumens, lux and lm/W.
Describe forward and reverse bias, why the colour depends on the material, and find the anode and cathode.
Work out and build LED circuits
Calculate a series resistor and its power rating, choose a standard value, and build series and parallel LED circuits correctly.
Explain and test LDRs, photodiodes, phototransistors and solar cells, and explain a dusk switch.
Say why an optocoupler is used, wire a seven-segment display, and explain laser classes and hazards.
Name the device used in remote controls, gate beams, photocells, barcode scanners, solar panels, fibre optics and smoke detectors.
Use the diode test and resistance ranges, find faults in LED and sensor circuits, and record the readings.
Use only the extra-low-voltage bench supply that the assessor connects, switch off before changes, control static, and protect your eyes from bright LEDs and lasers.

blocks.note: All practical work in this unit is done at **extra-low voltage** from a bench supply or battery, connected and switched on by the assessor. No mains is used. Switch off before you change anything in a circuit.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Read the sections in order, and work every example yourself before you read the answer. Keep a data sheet for each part you use. Then try the practice test and read each explanation.

sections.title: Light: what it is and how it is measured

blocks.p: Light is **electromagnetic radiation**, from the same family as radio waves and X-rays. It travels at about 300 000 km per second. Light of different **wavelengths** looks like different colours. Wavelengths of light are given in **nanometres (nm)**: 1 nm is one millionth of a millimetre.

head: Region
Wavelength (approximate)
Notes
rows: Invisible. Causes sunburn and eye damage. UV LEDs are used for curing glues and inks, checking banknotes and insect traps.
Blue LEDs, and the blue chip inside white LEDs
The eye is most sensitive to yellow-green light, around 555 nm
Indicator LEDs, traffic lights, laser pointers
Invisible. Remote controls (often about 850–940 nm), gate beams, fibre optics; at much longer wavelengths, the heat given off by warm bodies

blocks.p: The boundaries between colours are not sharp, so the figures are approximate. Visible light runs from roughly **400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red)**. Infrared has a **longer** wavelength than red; ultraviolet has a **shorter** wavelength than violet.

head: Quantity
Unit
What it means
Where you meet it

On the box of an LED lamp
lux (lx): 1 lux = 1 lumen per square metre
How much light falls on a surface
How bright a source is in one direction

Keep your body and shadow out of the way.
Read the value and compare it with the level advised for the task. Take readings at several points on a large surface.

blocks.h: Efficacy: why LED lighting saves money

blocks.p: A filament lamp turns most of its energy into heat; an LED turns much more of it into light. For the same light, an LED lamp uses about a sixth of the power. The lumen figure on the box tells you how much light you get; the watt figure tells you how much power it takes.

blocks.note: Electricity is expensive in Jamaica, so changing filament and fluorescent lamps to LED is one of the quickest ways for a home or business to cut its JPS bill. LEDs also put less heat into the room, which helps where air-conditioning is used.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Semiconductors** such as silicon conduct better than insulators but worse than metals. Adding tiny amounts of other elements (doping) makes **n-type** material, with spare electrons, and **p-type** material, with 'holes' where electrons are missing. Where the two meet is a **p-n junction**: the heart of every diode, LED, photodiode and solar cell.

ul: A diode has an **anode** (the p side) and a **cathode** (the n side). Its symbol is a triangle pointing at a bar; the bar is the cathode.
**Forward bias** (anode more positive than cathode): once the voltage passes about 0.6–0.7 V for a silicon diode, it conducts.
**Reverse bias** (cathode more positive): it blocks the current, apart from a tiny leakage, until the voltage is high enough to break it down.

blocks.h: How an LED gives out light

blocks.p: An **LED (light-emitting diode)** is a diode made from a semiconductor that gives out light. When it is forward biased, electrons cross the junction and drop into holes, and each gives up its energy as a tiny packet of light. **The semiconductor material sets the colour**: the energy each electron gives up decides the wavelength. Reverse biased, an LED blocks the current and does not light.

head: Colour
Typical wavelength
Typical forward voltage
Material
rows: A blue InGaN chip with a yellow phosphor coating

blocks.note: These are typical figures. The **data sheet** gives the real forward voltage, the largest current the LED can safely take (often about 20–30 mA for a 5 mm indicator LED), and the largest reverse voltage, which is often only about 5 V. Always read it.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Clue
Anode (+)
Cathode (−)
rows: Lead length on a new LED
Usually the larger, flag-shaped piece (not on every LED)
The red lead is on it when the LED glows faintly or reads its forward voltage
The black lead is on it then

blocks.p: Surface-mount LEDs carry a small mark at one end; the data sheet explains which end it is. Once leads have been cut, use the flat edge or the meter.

head: Device
Symbol
rows: A triangle pointing at a bar (the bar is the cathode)
The diode symbol with two small arrows pointing **away**: light goes out
The diode symbol with two arrows pointing **towards** it: light comes in
A transistor symbol with arrows pointing in
A resistor box, often in a circle, with arrows pointing in
An LED and a phototransistor drawn in one box, with arrows between them

head: Good points of LEDs
What needs care
rows: Much more light per watt, so lower bills
Long life, often 15 000–50 000 hours against about 1000 for a filament lamp
Tough: no glass bulb or filament to break
Light at once, in many colours, from a small size
The current must be limited, by a resistor or a driver
They work on DC, the right way round
The chip still makes some heat: power LEDs need a heat sink or they fail early
Mains LED lamps need a driver inside, which must suit any dimmer used

blocks.p: A filament lamp limits its own current; an LED does not. Above its forward voltage, a small rise in voltage makes a large rise in current, and the LED burns out. So every LED needs something to **limit its current**: for indicator LEDs, a **series resistor** that drops the rest of the supply voltage.
**R = (supply voltage − LED forward voltage) ÷ LED current**, with the current in amps (15 mA = 0.015 A). The power the resistor turns into heat is **P = (voltage across the resistor) × current**.

flow: Read the LED's forward voltage and current from the data sheet
Take the LED's voltage away from the supply voltage: that is the resistor's voltage
Divide by the current in amps to find R
Choose the next standard value above R
Work out the resistor's power and choose a rating of about twice that or more
Build with the supply off; after switch-on, measure and compare

blocks.p: **Example 1.** A red LED (2.0 V, 15 mA) on a 5 V supply. Resistor voltage = 5 − 2 = 3 V. R = 3 ÷ 0.015 = 200 Ω. The next standard value up is 220 Ω, giving I = 3 ÷ 220 ≈ 13.6 mA. Power = 3 × 0.0136 ≈ 0.04 W, so a 0.25 W resistor is plenty.

**Example 2.** Two white LEDs in series (3.2 V each, 20 mA) on 12 V. The LEDs need 6.4 V, leaving 12 − 6.4 = 5.6 V for the resistor. R = 5.6 ÷ 0.02 = 280 Ω; fit 330 Ω, giving about 17 mA. Power = 5.6 × 0.017 ≈ 0.1 W: a 0.25 W resistor will do.

Resistors are made in standard values. The E12 series repeats in every decade: **10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82** (then 100, 120, 150 … 820, 1 k, 1.2 k and so on). Choose the next value **above** the one you worked out: the current comes out a little lower, which is safer and makes almost no difference to the brightness.

ul: The **same current** flows through every LED, so one resistor sets the current for the whole string.

The LED voltages **add up**: three red LEDs at 2 V need 6 V. The supply must be higher than the total, with some voltage left for the resistor. Four white LEDs (about 12.8 V) will not light properly on a 12 V supply.
If one LED fails open, the whole string goes out.

blocks.p: Give **each LED (or each series string) its own resistor**. No two LEDs have exactly the same forward voltage. With one shared resistor, the LED with the lowest forward voltage takes most of the current, gets hotter, takes even more, and fails; then the others share the current and fail in turn. Separate resistors make each LED share the current fairly.

ul: **Reverse voltage**: many LEDs are damaged by more than about 5 V in reverse. If an LED could see reverse voltage, for example on AC, fit a protecting diode as the circuit drawing shows.
**Dimming**: a larger resistor lowers the current and the brightness. Electronic dimmers switch the LED on and off very quickly (pulse-width modulation); the eye sees the average.

**Measuring**: measure the current with the meter in **series** with the LED, and the voltages across the LED and the resistor with the meter in **parallel**. The two voltages should add up to the supply voltage.

blocks.note: Write your worked-out values in a results table before you build. After the assessor switches on, add the measured values beside them. A big difference tells you something is wrong: a wrong resistor, an LED backwards, or a loose wire.
blocks.label: Tip

Dusk-to-dawn switches, night lights, light-level sensing
Connected in **reverse bias**; a small current flows that rises with the light
Fibre-optic receivers, remote-control receivers, light meters, smoke detectors

blocks.p: A dusk switch turns a light on when it gets dark. The LDR and a fixed resistor are connected in series across the supply to form a **voltage divider**. The point between them feeds the base of an NPN transistor, which switches an LED, lamp or relay.

ul: With the **LDR between the base and 0 V**: in daylight its resistance is low, so the base voltage is low (below about 0.6 V) and the transistor is off.
At dusk the LDR's resistance **rises**, so it takes a bigger share of the supply voltage. The base voltage rises past about 0.6–0.7 V, the transistor switches on, and the light comes on.
Swap the LDR and the fixed resistor round and you have a light-activated switch instead.
A variable resistor in place of the fixed one lets you set how dark it must get before the light comes on.

flow: It gets dark
The LDR's resistance rises
The voltage across the LDR (the base voltage) rises
It passes about 0.6–0.7 V
The transistor switches on
The light comes on

blocks.note: Fit the sensor where it sees the daylight but **not the light it controls**. If the lamp's own light reaches the sensor, the lamp switches itself off, then on again as soon as it is dark: it flickers all evening.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: The order of a transistor's leads (emitter, base, collector) depends on the type and the package. Always check the data sheet before you connect it.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: A solar cell is a thin slice of semiconductor, usually silicon, with a junction inside it, like a large flat diode. Light frees electrons, and the junction drives them one way, so a **direct current** flows in a load.
One silicon cell gives only about **0.5–0.6 V**. Its current depends on its size and how bright the light is.
Cells joined in **series** add their voltages. A panel of 36 cells gives about 18 V when working, which suits charging a 12 V battery through a charge controller. Larger panels have 60 or more cells.
Cells or panels joined in **parallel** (positive to positive, negative to negative) add their currents at the same voltage.

Because the cells in a string are in series, **shade on even one cell** limits the current of the whole string. Bypass diodes in the panel's junction box reduce the loss, but the best answer is no shade.
Panels give DC. An inverter is needed to run ordinary 110 V or 220 V AC appliances.
Keep panels clean: dust and bird droppings cut the output. Panels also give a little less voltage when they are very hot.

blocks.p: An **optocoupler** is a small package with an **LED** on one side and a light sensor, usually a **phototransistor**, on the other, facing each other in the dark. There is no wire between them. When current flows through the LED, its light switches on the phototransistor, so a signal passes across **by light only**.

ul: It keeps two circuits **electrically apart** (isolated), often up to several thousand volts: the data sheet gives the figure.
It protects a small, delicate control circuit from high voltages, electrical noise and surges in the circuit it is connected to, and it protects the person using the control side.
Uses: the feedback in switch-mode power supplies, the inputs of PLCs, a small controller switching a relay or motor drive, and the beam inputs on gate controllers.
Some optocouplers have a light-operated triac or a photodiode on the output side instead.

Related devices: a **slotted optical switch** has an LED and sensor on either side of a slot, so that anything passing through the slot breaks the light; a **reflective sensor** sees light bounced back from a surface. They count, sense position and measure speed.

blocks.p: Pin 1 of an optocoupler is marked with a dot or notch. On common types the LED's anode and cathode are pins 1 and 2, and the output transistor is on the other side. Check the data sheet.

A seven-segment display has seven bar-shaped LEDs, named **a** to **g**, and usually a decimal point (dp). Segment a is the top bar; b and c run down the right side; d is the bottom; e and f run up the left side; g is the middle bar. Lighting different segments makes the figures 0 to 9.

head: Type
The common pin goes to
A segment lights when its pin is
rows: Taken towards 0 V (low), through its resistor

ul: Each segment is an LED, so each needs its **own current-limiting resistor**.
Other displays: **dot-matrix** LED displays and LED video panels made of red, green and blue LEDs; **LCDs**, which do not give out light and need a backlight, usually LEDs.

blocks.p: A **laser** gives out light of **one colour** (one wavelength) in a **narrow, concentrated beam** that hardly spreads. An ordinary LED gives a wide glow of a spread of wavelengths. Small **laser diodes** are used in barcode scanners, laser levels, fibre-optic transmitters, printers, disc players and pointers. Because all the power is packed into a tiny spot, a laser can damage the eye, sometimes in under a second.

head: Laser class
What it means
rows: Safe in normal use (often because the laser is enclosed, as in a printer)
Low-power visible beam. The natural blink gives some protection against a brief accident, but never stare into it or point it at anyone.
Higher power: avoid any direct eye exposure
Direct beam is hazardous to the eye: controlled use and eye protection
Can burn eyes and skin and start fires: specialists only

blocks.note: Never look into a laser beam or the end of a fibre, and never point a laser at anyone. Infrared lasers used in fibre optics are **invisible**, so the eye gets no warning and does not blink. Read the class on the label, aim beams at a dull surface where they cannot reflect off metal, glass or watches, and switch lasers off when not in use. Cheap pointers are sometimes stronger than their labels say.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Once you know the devices, you will see them everywhere.

How it works

Infrared LED; receiver module with a photodiode
The remote sends coded pulses of infrared; the receiver decodes them
Photocell (LDR or photodiode); often a PIR sensor too
On at dusk, off at dawn; the PIR switches on when someone moves
Infrared LED transmitter; phototransistor or photodiode receiver; optocouplers on the control board
A car or person breaking the beam stops or reverses the gate
Barcode scanner: a laser or LED and a light sensor
Dark bars reflect little light and white spaces a lot; the sensor reads the pattern
Panels on homes, schools and businesses; solar garden and street lights
Fibre-optic cables with laser or LED transmitters and photodiode receivers
Data travels as pulses of light
Infrared LED and photodiode in a dark chamber
Smoke scatters the LED's light onto the photodiode and sets off the alarm
Shop signs, gas station price boards, traffic lights
Optocouplers, light curtains, slotted and reflective sensors
Isolating controls, guarding machines, counting goods on conveyors
Red and infrared LEDs with a photodiode
A pulse oximeter clipped on a finger measures oxygen in the blood

blocks.note: Strong sunshine all year makes solar panels attractive here, and high electricity costs have pushed many homes and businesses to LED lighting. As an electrician you will be asked to fit, check and repair both, so the basics in this unit matter.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Safe working, testing and fault finding

ul: Use **only** the extra-low-voltage bench supply or battery the assessor gives you. Only the assessor connects and switches the supply. Never use the mains for these circuits.
**Switch off before you change anything.** Check with your meter that the supply rails read 0 V before you pull out or push in a part.
Wear an anti-static wrist strap when you handle chips, transistors and optocouplers: static from your body can damage the tiny chip inside.
When soldering LEDs and sensors, touch each joint for only a few seconds, and hold the lead with pliers as a heat sink: too much heat damages the chip.
Cut leads are sharp and fly: point them down when you cut, and put the off-cuts in a container.
Do not stare into bright LEDs: look at them from the side or through a diffuser. UV LEDs can harm eyes and skin: use them only as the instructor directs.
A desk lamp used for light tests gets hot: do not touch the shade, and keep it away from paper.
A **breadboard** lets you build trial circuits without solder. Under each short row of five holes is a metal strip that joins them.
A channel runs down the middle. The rows on each side of it are separate, so chips sit across it.
The long **power rails** along the edges carry the supply. On some boards the rails are split halfway along: check with a meter, or bridge them.
Use red wires for positive and black for 0 V, and keep wires short and flat so that the circuit is easy to check.

flow: Draw the circuit and read the data sheets
Work out the resistor values; have the instructor check them
Check each part: read the resistor colour code and confirm it with the meter
Build with the supply off, with every LED the right way round
Check the wiring against the drawing, then ask the assessor to check it
The assessor connects the supply and switches on
Measure voltages and currents and record them beside the worked-out values
Switch off before any change; at the end, take the circuit apart, return the parts and clean the bench

A faulty part

OL both ways: open. Near 0 both ways: shorted.
White, blue or bright green LED

About 2.6–3.2 V one way, if the meter can supply enough voltage
Some meters cannot light these LEDs and show OL both ways even when they are good: test in a circuit with a resistor on the bench supply
High when covered, falling a long way under a lamp

blocks.note: On a manual-range meter, choose the lowest range above the value you expect. An LDR in the dark may read several hundred kilohms or more: on the 200 kΩ range that shows OL, so move up to the 2 MΩ range.

blocks.p: Your report should give the circuit drawing, the worked-out values, the measured readings in a table, any faults you found and what you did to put them right. Readings without units, or a report that only says 'it worked', are not enough.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

What it is

terms: Anode
The positive lead of a diode or LED; on a new LED, the longer lead.
Breadboard
A board with rows of connected holes for building trial circuits without solder.
Cathode
The negative lead of a diode or LED; marked by the flat edge on a round LED.
Common anode / common cathode
Displays whose segment anodes (or cathodes) are joined to one pin.
Efficacy
Light given out for each watt of power, in lumens per watt.
Forward bias
Anode more positive than cathode, so a diode conducts.
Infrared
Light with a longer wavelength than red, which the eye cannot see.
Laser
A source of a narrow, concentrated beam of light of one colour.
LDR
Light-dependent resistor: its resistance falls as light increases.
LED
Light-emitting diode: a diode that gives out light when forward biased.
Lumen
The unit of the total light a source gives out.
Lux
The unit of light falling on a surface: one lumen per square metre.
Nanometre (nm)
One millionth of a millimetre; the unit for wavelengths of light.
Optocoupler
An LED and a light sensor in one package, passing a signal by light while keeping two circuits apart.
Photodiode
A diode, used in reverse bias, that lets a current flow when light falls on it.
Phototransistor
A transistor switched on by light instead of a base current.
Photovoltaic effect
Light falling on a material making a voltage, as in a solar cell.
Reverse bias
Cathode more positive than anode, so a diode blocks the current.
Seven-segment display
A display of seven bars of light that shows the figures 0 to 9.
Ultraviolet
Light with a shorter wavelength than violet, which the eye cannot see.
Voltage divider
Two resistances in series across a supply, sharing its voltage; used to set a transistor's base voltage.

c1.title: Indicator lamps for a Lucea school pump
c1.text: At a primary school in Lucea, Hanover, the caretaker wants two indicator LEDs on the 12 V DC control box of the water pump: green for 'pump running' and red for 'tank low'. Trainee Javaun reads the data sheets: the green LED needs about 2.2 V at 15 mA, and the red LED about 2.0 V at 15 mA. The workshop stocks E12 resistors in 0.25 W and 0.5 W ratings.

c2.title: A dusk light at a Treasure Beach guest house
c2.text: Mrs Beverley Clarke runs a guest house at Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth. Trainee Shanique is checking a small 12 V dusk-switch board for the gate light. On the board, the light-dependent resistor (LDR) is connected between the transistor's base and 0 V, with a fixed resistor from the base to +12 V. On the bench the LDR reads about 900 kΩ when covered and about 400 Ω under a lamp. Once fitted at the gate, the light comes on at dusk, then keeps flicking off and on all evening.

c3.title: Solar lights for a goat farm near Kellits
c3.text: Mr Desmond Wright keeps goats near Kellits, Clarendon, where his shed has no JPS supply. He buys a solar panel made of 36 silicon cells, a battery, a charge controller and LED lights. The panel is fixed on the shed roof, where a mango tree shades one corner of it in the afternoon. Later he asks how to get more charging current.

c4.title: A gate beam at a Red Hills townhouse complex
c4.text: The sliding gate at a townhouse complex in Red Hills, St Andrew, has an infrared safety beam: a transmitter on one post and a receiver on the other. Residents complain that the gate will not close, mostly in the late afternoon, when the sun shines straight into the receiver. Trainee Omar, working with a gate technician, can see no light at all coming from the transmitter. On the gate's control board, a six-pin optocoupler sits between the beam input and the small controller chip.

c5.title: Testing parts in the Kingston lab
c5.text: In the electronics lab at the Centre in Kingston, trainee Tamara tests parts from a returned kit. Her meter's diode test gives no more than about 2.6 V. A red LED reads 1.82 V one way and OL the other. A white LED reads OL both ways. A seven-segment display in the kit is marked 'common anode'. Her classmate has brought in a red laser pointer labelled Class 2.

questions.q: What resistor value does Javaun work out for the green LED?
o: About 6.5 Ω
About 653 Ω
About 147 Ω
About 800 Ω
questions.why: R = (supply − LED voltage) ÷ current = (12 − 2.2) ÷ 0.015 = 9.8 ÷ 0.015 ≈ 653 Ω. 800 Ω forgets to take off the LED's voltage; 147 Ω uses the LED's voltage instead of the resistor's.

questions.q: Which E12 value should he fit for the green LED?
o: 6.8 kΩ
questions.why: Choose the next standard value above the worked-out figure: 680 Ω, which gives about 14 mA, a little under the 15 mA. 560 Ω would let more current flow, 650 Ω is not an E12 value, and 6.8 kΩ is ten times too big, so the LED would be very dim.

questions.q: With 680 Ω, the resistor drops 9.8 V at about 14.4 mA. Which power rating is the better choice?
o: 0.25 W, since it is just above the power
0.5 W, to give a safe margin
5 W, as bigger is always better
0.125 W, the smallest that would fit
questions.why: P = V × I = 9.8 × 0.0144 ≈ 0.14 W. A 0.25 W resistor would run close to its limit and get hot in a closed box; choosing about twice the worked-out power, here 0.5 W, keeps it cool. A 5 W resistor works but is large and wasteful.

questions.q: The red LED glows only faintly. The resistor fitted beside it has the bands blue, grey, red. What is wrong?
o: It is 6.8 kΩ, not 680 Ω: too little current flows
It is 6.8 kΩ, which is right; the LED is just weak
It is 68 Ω, so far too much current is flowing
It is 680 Ω, so the red LED must be fitted backwards
questions.why: Blue (6), grey (8), red (× 100) = 6800 Ω = 6.8 kΩ. The current is about (12 − 2) ÷ 6800 ≈ 1.5 mA, a tenth of what it should be, so the LED is dim. A 680 Ω resistor is blue, grey, brown. A reversed LED would not light at all.

questions.q: Why does the light come on when it gets dark?
o: The LDR's resistance falls, so the base voltage rises
The LDR's resistance rises, so the base voltage rises
The LDR makes its own voltage when it is in the dark
The transistor senses the darkness through its case
questions.why: The LDR and the fixed resistor share the 12 V. In the dark the LDR's resistance rises, so it takes a bigger share and the base voltage rises past about 0.6–0.7 V, switching the transistor and the light on. In daylight its resistance falls, the base voltage falls and the transistor turns off.

questions.q: Why does the gate light keep flicking off and on?
o: The lamp's own light falls on the LDR
The LDR reacts too slowly to the dusk
The 12 V supply is too high for the LDR
The LDR has been fitted the wrong way round
questions.why: When the lamp comes on, its light reaches the LDR, so the circuit 'sees' daylight and switches the lamp off; then it is dark again, and the cycle repeats. Fit or shade the LDR so that it sees the sky but not the lamp. An LDR has no polarity, so it cannot be the wrong way round.

questions.q: Shanique's meter has manual ranges. Which resistance range should she choose to read the covered LDR?
o: 200 kΩ
2 kΩ
2 MΩ
questions.why: Pick the lowest range above the value you expect. About 900 kΩ is above the 200 kΩ range, which would show OL; the 2 MΩ range reads it. Use the lower ranges for the LDR in bright light.

questions.q: About what voltage does the panel give when it is working in good sun?
o: About 18 V
About 36 V
About 0.5 V
About 9 V
questions.why: The cells are in series, so their voltages add: 36 × about 0.5 V ≈ 18 V when working (a little more with no load). This is the usual size of panel for charging a 12 V battery through a charge controller.

questions.q: Why does the shade on one corner cut the panel's output so much?
o: Shaded cells turn the light that falls on them into heat
The leaves reflect the infrared light away from the cells
The cells are in series, so a shaded cell limits all
Shade makes the panel give out AC instead of DC current
questions.why: In a series string the same current flows through every cell, so a shaded cell limits the current of the whole string. Bypass diodes in the panel's junction box let the current go round shaded groups and reduce the loss, but the best cure is a place with no shade, or trimming the tree.

questions.q: Mr Wright adds a second panel just like the first, to get more current at the same voltage. How should the two panels be joined?
o: Only the positives joined; negatives left free
Positive to positive and negative to negative
Positive of each to the other panel's negative
Positive of one panel to negative of the other
questions.why: Joined in parallel, positive to positive and negative to negative, the panels keep the same voltage and their currents add. Positive of one to negative of the other joins them in series, which doubles the voltage instead; joining each positive to the other's negative short-circuits them.

questions.q: Omar can see no light coming from the transmitter. Why does that not prove it is faulty?
o: It shines only when a car is in front of it
Its ultraviolet light is too dim for the eye to see
Its infrared light cannot be seen by the eye
It only shines at night, when it is really needed
questions.why: Gate beams use infrared, which has a longer wavelength than red light and cannot be seen. You need another way to check that it is sending, such as a camera, a beam tester or the receiver's indicator lamp.

questions.q: Which is a quick way for Omar to check that the transmitter is sending?
o: Touch the lens to feel whether it is warm
Hold a lux meter in front of its lens
Look at it through a phone camera screen
Shine a torch into the receiver's lens
questions.why: Many phone cameras pick up near-infrared and show a working IR LED as a faint purple-white glow (if the back camera filters it out, try the front one). A lux meter is made to read visible light, and an IR LED is barely warm.

questions.q: Why does the gate fail mostly when the late-afternoon sun shines into the receiver?
o: The optocoupler works only in the dark
The heat makes the transmitter LED shine more brightly
Sunlight has strong infrared that swamps the beam
Sunlight bends the infrared beam away from it
questions.why: Sunlight contains a lot of infrared. Shining straight into the receiver, it can swamp the transmitter's signal, so the controller treats the beam as blocked and will not close the gate. A hood, shading, or turning the receiver away from the low sun usually cures it.

questions.q: A lightning surge comes in on the beam cable, but the controller chip survives. Which part most likely protected it?
o: The receiver's photodiode, as it blocks surges
The infrared LED in the beam transmitter
The gate motor's limit switch at the end of travel
The optocoupler, as only light crosses inside it
questions.why: Inside an optocoupler the signal crosses a small gap as light, with no wire between the two sides. A surge on the beam side may destroy the optocoupler, but the controller on the other side is kept apart from it, often up to several thousand volts.

questions.q: Tamara decides that the white LED is open circuit. Why might she be wrong?
o: White LEDs can only be tested with the leads reversed
White LEDs give out infrared, so they always read OL
White LEDs are not diodes, so a diode test cannot work
A white LED may need more than her meter gives
questions.why: White (and blue) LEDs need about 3 V to conduct. A meter whose diode test gives only about 2.6 V cannot turn one on, so it shows OL both ways even when the LED is good. Test it instead in a simple circuit with a resistor on the bench supply, or with a meter that gives a higher test voltage.

questions.q: How should Tamara connect the common pin of the common-anode display?
o: To each segment's resistor
To nothing; it is a spare
To the positive supply
To 0 V (negative)
questions.why: In a common-anode display all the segment anodes are joined to one pin, which goes to the positive supply. Each segment lights when its own pin is taken low (towards 0 V) through its resistor. A common-cathode display is the other way round.

questions.q: What does the 'Class 2' label on the laser pointer tell the class?
o: It is safe to stare into the beam for any length of time
It gives infrared, so its beam cannot be seen
It is high power and can burn skin and start fires
Low power, but the beam must still not go into eyes
questions.why: Class 2 lasers give low-power visible light. The natural blink usually protects the eye from a brief accident, but staring into the beam or shining it at people is still dangerous. Higher classes (3R, 3B, 4) are more hazardous, and cheap pointers are sometimes stronger than their labels say.

questions.q: A trainee measures 180 lux on a soldering bench. About 750 to 1000 lux is advised for fine work. What should be done?
o: Add task lighting over the bench and re-measure
Use a soldering iron with a hotter tip
Hold the lux meter nearer the ceiling lamp
Nothing, since any reading over 100 lux is enough
questions.why: 180 lux is far too dark for fine soldering: you would strain your eyes and make mistakes. Add a lamp over the work and measure again, with the sensor flat on the bench where the work is done, not raised towards the lamp.

questions.q: An LED lamp gives 800 lumens and takes 9 W. About what is its efficacy?
o: About 89 lm/W
About 13 lm/W
About 0.01 lm/W
About 7200 lm/W
questions.why: Efficacy = lumens ÷ watts = 800 ÷ 9 ≈ 89 lm/W. A filament lamp giving the same 800 lumens takes about 60 W, only about 13 lm/W, because most of its energy becomes heat.

questions.q: Three white LEDs, each needing 3.1 V at 20 mA, are wired in series with one resistor on a 12 V supply. What resistor is needed?
o: About 445 Ω; fit 470 Ω
About 45 Ω; fit 47 Ω
About 600 Ω; fit 680 Ω
About 135 Ω; fit 150 Ω
questions.why: The LEDs in series need 3 × 3.1 = 9.3 V, leaving 12 − 9.3 = 2.7 V for the resistor. The same 20 mA flows through all of them, so R = 2.7 ÷ 0.02 = 135 Ω; fit the next value up, 150 Ω. 445 Ω counts only one LED, and 45 Ω wrongly triples the current.
